summary: Summation No. 18 covers March 1947, the month before the first national and local elections under the new Constitution. MacArthur told foreign correspondents on 17 March that the United Nations should take over the occupation after a peace treaty, and on 22 March sent Prime Minister Yoshida a letter demanding firm Japanese action on food collection, rationing, wages, prices and inflation. The 92nd Diet adjourned on 31 March after passing the Fundamental Law of Education, School Education Law, Labor Standards Law, Local Autonomy Law, new tax laws, a revised House of Representatives election law and an anti-monopoly (Fair Trade) law, while the Progressive Party and Liberal defectors merged into the Japan Democratic Party. The IMTFE defence closed its general phase and opened the Manchurian phase. Economic sections report coal-limited production, a new rice-delivery bonus scheme, labor federations uniting, and extensive statistical tables on industry, finance, health and education. Historians will find election platforms, legislative tables, war-crimes trial results and detailed production figures useful.
highlights: On 17 March MacArthur told Tokyo foreign press that the political and military phases of the occupation were substantially complete and that the United Nations should assume responsibility after a peace treaty, using 'protective rather than repressive' controls.

MacArthur's 22 March letter to Yoshida invoked Directive No. 3 of 22 September 1945, warned that the Allied powers had no obligation to import food to cover Japanese maldistribution, and called for integrated economic controls through the Economic Stabilization Board.

The Japan Democratic Party formed on 31 March with 145 Diet members (114 Progressives, 17 People's Cooperatives, eight Liberals, six independents), overtaking the Liberals' 142; the People's Cooperative Party had formed on 8 March.

The House of Representatives election law was revised on 30-31 March: 117 districts replaced 53, each voter casts one vote for three to five seats, and candidate deposits rose from 2,000 to 5,000 yen, after a filibuster and scuffle on 27 March.

The 92nd Diet adjourned 31 March having passed 77 government measures and 10 member bills, including the Labor Standards Law (27 March), Fundamental Law of Education, Local Autonomy Law (28 March), Securities and Exchange Law and Fair Trade Commission law.

A new rice bonus plan paid 150 yen per koku above 80 percent of quota delivered by 31 March and 300 yen per koku over quota by 30 April; by 10 March about 85 percent of farmers had met quotas, and tonari-gumi food distribution ended 1 April.

Six war-crimes trials involving 12 defendants ended in Japan with sentences up to 40 years; seven Philippine trials brought totals to 196 tried and 181 convicted, and 131 more suspects were ordered apprehended for Sugamo.

Bank of Japan notes in circulation reached 115,726,000,000 yen on 31 March; 1947-48 budgets of 114.5 billion yen (general account) and 124.9 billion (special accounts) were authorized, with income tax moved to pay-as-you-go and self-assessment.

sections.title: Front matter
sections.summary: Cover of Summation No. 18 for March 1947, contents for Parts I-IV, and the list of 97 charts, maps and graphs.

sections.title: Part I: General
sections.summary: Monthly digest: no change in SCAP organization, MacArthur's UN statement, the new Democratic Party, Diet adjournment, economic output, labor laws, finance and social developments.

sections.title: Section 1. Organization Under SCAP
sections.summary: States there was no change in the non-military organization of GHQ SCAP during March 1947.

sections.title: Section 2. Political Activities
sections.summary: MacArthur's 22 March letter to Yoshida, formation of the People's Cooperative and Japan Democratic parties, 92nd Diet adjournment on 31 March, and Takase named Economic Stabilization Board head.

sections.title: Section 3. Economic Activities
sections.summary: Natural resources, industry, labor, trade, rationing, finance and property control, including 28,000 houses completed in February and a 22 March release of 173,561 pairs of shoes.

sections.title: Section 4. Social Activities
sections.summary: Meningitis rose to 282 cases; 64,898 repatriates; Fundamental Law of Education, shrine land law, election publicity and 581,207 educational film viewers.

sections.title: Part II: Political
sections.summary: MacArthur's statements, the election campaign and new parties, Diet legislation, local government reform, public safety, and war-crimes proceedings including the IMTFE defence phases.

sections.title: Section 1. Government and Politics
sections.summary: MacArthur-Yoshida letters, platforms for the April elections, the Democratic Party's formation, election law revision, 92nd Diet legislation tables, the purge amendment and local government law.

sections.title: Supreme Commander Advocates United Nations Control
sections.summary: MacArthur's 17 March luncheon remarks urging UN supervision after a peace treaty, with Yoshida's praise and Asahi and Mainichi editorials.

sections.title: Economic Reforms: MacArthur-Yoshida Letters
sections.summary: MacArthur's 22 March letter citing Directive No. 3; Yoshida's six-point reply promising 110 percent rice collection and 30,000,000 tons of coal; party reactions.

sections.title: Election Campaign
sections.summary: Liberal, Progressive and Communist platforms, a joint emergency program, and legal limits on campaign spending, postcards and posters for the April elections.

sections.title: New Political Parties
sections.summary: People's Cooperative Party formed 8 March, Workers' Vanguard Party 9 March, and Japan Democratic Party 31 March with 145 Diet members.

sections.title: The Diet
sections.summary: Election law revision creating 117 districts, the 27 March scuffle, and tables of government and member bills passed by the 92nd Diet.

sections.title: The Purge
sections.summary: Imperial Ordinance No. 1 of 1947 amended to bar purgees from campaigning, with 72-hour screening decisions; a party committee formed 14 March to help administer the purge.

sections.title: The Central Government
sections.summary: Communications Ministry graft dispute involving Minister Hitotsumatsu and 300 resignations, Ushio's State Planning post, and Takase's appointment after Wada declined.

sections.title: Local Government
sections.summary: Law of Local Government enacted 28 March, merging four laws into 300 articles, ending the Home Minister's power to dismiss governors and adding initiative and referendum.

sections.title: Section 2. Public Safety
sections.summary: Fewer labor demonstrations, black-market crackdown, 111,328 offenses in January, 970 railway suicides, amnesty effects on 38,115 prisoners, and January fire losses of 302,966,754 yen.

sections.title: Section 3. Legal and War Crimes
sections.summary: Chinese nationals' status, 161 new atrocity cases, 131 suspects to be apprehended, trial results in Japan and the Philippines, and IMTFE defence witnesses and the Manchurian phase.

sections.title: International Prosecution of War Criminals
sections.summary: Defence closed its general phase on 18 March with treaties and witnesses Fujita, Okada, Mitarai and Tamura, then opened the Manchurian phase with the Lytton Report on 19 March.

sections.title: Part III: Economic
sections.summary: Production, trade, labor, rationing, finance and property statistics for February-March 1947, dominated by coal, power and raw-material shortages and the rice collection drive.

sections.title: Section 1. Agriculture and Fisheries
sections.summary: Land commission elections 20-25 February, 442 recall elections, rice bonus scheme, February fish landings of 75,227 tons, Antarctic whaling, and game laws revised effective 15 April.

sections.title: Section 2. Forestry and Mining
sections.summary: February log output of 685,144,000 board feet, 20,279 sawmills, reforestation of 517,000 acres, and February coal output of 2,028,700 tons.

sections.title: Section 3. Heavy Industries
sections.summary: February coke of 106,400 tons, iron and steel hit by short coal deliveries, aluminum 863 tons, cement, record housing construction, and new technical research committees.

sections.title: Section 4. Manufacturing
sections.summary: Pulp output down 1,681 tons, camera output up 200 percent, plus food processing, paper, glass, medicines, electrical goods, rubber and leather; agricultural equipment limited by steel plate shortage.

sections.title: Section 5. Textile Industries
sections.summary: February cotton yarn of 25,041,000 pounds with 55 of 59 mills meeting quotas, raw silk 8,252 bales, and wool yarn limited by power.

sections.title: Section 6. Transportation and Public Utilities
sections.summary: Motor vehicles fell to 112,155, railway freight reached 7,567,600 tons, and power generated was 2,010,305,000 kWh despite a hydro drop.

sections.title: Section 7. Communications
sections.summary: Order of 25 March to liquidate the International Telecommunications Company, accrual accounting law, telephone and telegraph rate rises, radio licensees, and postal services.

sections.title: Section 8. Labor
sections.summary: Labor Standards Law enacted 27 March, National Liaison Council of unions formed 10 March, government workers' dispute settled 27 February, plus labor relations committees, wages and employment.

sections.title: Section 9. Imports and Exports
sections.summary: February imports included about 50,000 tons of salt; first exports of cloth woven from imported cotton went to Hongkong and the Netherlands East Indies.

sections.title: Section 10. Rationing and Price Control
sections.summary: Government held 69.9 days of staple food on 28 February; 3,686,633 tons of rice collected under a 110 percent collection order; fertilizer, coal, lumber and cement allocation; price violations.

sections.title: Section 11. Finance
sections.summary: Bank of Japan notes of 115,726,000,000 yen, six new tax laws including pay-as-you-go income tax, and 1947-48 budgets passed by the Diet.

sections.title: Section 12. Property Control and Reparations
sections.summary: Restitution directives for foreign-owned properties, 914 reports on overseas Japanese corporations, British property analysis, dissolved ultranationalist organizations and precious metals held by SCAP.

sections.title: Part IV: Social
sections.summary: Public health, welfare, repatriation, vital statistics, education reform, religion and media, including the Fundamental Law of Education and election publicity.

sections.title: Section 1. Public Health and Welfare
sections.summary: February nutrition survey showing 1,921 calories in Tokyo, 282 meningitis cases, DDT production, welfare aid to 2,701,670, and a tuberculosis plan, narcotics reregistration and repatriation.

sections.title: Section 2. Education, Religion and Media of Expression
sections.summary: Fundamental Law of Education (25 March), new curriculums, shrine and temple land law, removal of militaristic monuments, and election information programs.

sections.title: Map of Japan
sections.summary: Closing map of Japan with prefectural boundaries.
